correctness.rationale: Exact two-point unit-edge integrations yield both moments. The line-graph excess identity is algebraically exact. The degree-sequence majorization and pair-incidence lower bound put the nonincident-edge probability between explicit endpoints; the conditional-variance inequality is elementary and yields the sharp second-minimum with a proved unique equality shape. A standalone exact enumerator verified 19,544 finite trees and direct shortest-route midpoint quadratures; these are supplementary and not substituted for the universal proof.

broader_coverage.reasoning: Mean-distance extremality and stochastic ordering are logically weaker in this direction: stochastic dominance does not imply variance dominance. The new proof additionally constrains both the lower and upper possible mass of nonincident edge pairs and derives an exact conditional-variance stability bound. It specifies a unique second-best shape and exact gap not in the identified broader first-moment results.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: First-order stochastic comparison controls the integral of the survival function but not the centered second moment. For example a Bernoulli(1/2) random variable is stochastically no larger than constant 1, but has larger variance. A sharp first-mean gap fixes an average excess but does not force the conditional variance term or the required upper mass bound. The central new implication proves those additional restrictions over all tree topologies.

value.rationale: For a natural geometric sampling model, the result exactly identifies the optimal network shape and the unique nearest competitor for variance rather than mean. Its sharp positive gap for every edge count and nonnegative variance-surplus identity explain the role of nonincident edge pairs and rule out a simple deduction from first-moment stochastic extremality. It is a complete, motivated second-minimum classification, not an arbitrary finite numerical slice.
